title: Overdispersion in counts and binaries
dek: If Var(Y) exceeds the exponential-family script, SEs and p-values from φ = 1 are too small. The mean model may still be fine.
story: Poisson says Var = μ. Binomial says Var = nπ(1−π). Real TB case counts, cluster sizes, and even binary outcomes with unmodelled clusters, overshoot. The Pearson dispersion φ̂ = X² / df is the first alarm, not a diagnosis.

Diagnosis splits: (1) wrong mean (missing curvature, missing offset, outliers) inflates residuals; (2) genuine extra-Poisson heterogeneity. Residual plots and a better mean come before a second variance parameter.

Scientific sources of extra variance in this lab: household clustering, lab batches, bursts of transmission, heteroresistance mixtures. Those are hierarchical or mixture likelihoods, of which quasi-φ is a blunt average.
deepTitle: NB, mixed Poisson, and what φ cannot see
deep: Negative binomial: Y | λ ~ Poisson(λ), λ ~ Gamma, so Var = μ + μ²/k. The quadratic term matters in the tail. Quasi-Poisson keeps Var = φμ, linear in μ. Predictions and weights disagree when μ spans decades (RNA-seq, district populations).
Random-intercept Poisson: Var_marginal(Y) > E[Y] automatically. That overdispersion has a name (τ²) and a clustering unit. φ̂ from a GLM that ignored clusters is a smear of τ².
Underdispersion exists (Var < μ) in tightly regulated assays. Quasi φ̂ < 1 then inflates precision if you naively take it; check the assay before celebrating.

Binary overdispersion at n_i = 1 is not identifiable as φ in a Bernoulli GLM (φ is not free). Extra-binomial variation needs replicated binomials (n_i > 1) or a random effect. Do not quote quasi-binomial φ on unique Bernoulli rows.

formulas.label: Pearson dispersion
formulas.note: ≈1 if the variance function is right and the mean is not badly wrong.

formulas.label: NB variance
formulas.note: k → ∞ recovers Poisson. Quasi-Poisson instead uses φμ.

visual.caption: Variance recipes against μ. Poisson is the diagonal Var=μ. Quasi-Poisson is a steeper line. Negative binomial bends up. A mixed Poisson sits somewhere depending on τ². Pick with a residual plot and a clustering story, not a smallest p.

example.title: φ̂ = 3.5 on district counts
example.setup: Poisson GLM for annual RR-TB counts by district, offset log(population). Pearson φ̂ = 3.5. Two large districts had outbreaks.

steps.title: Do not stop at φ
steps.body: Add an outbreak year term or a random intercept for district. If φ̂ falls toward 1, the extra variance had a name.

steps.title: If φ̂ stays high
steps.body: Quasi-Poisson or NB. With a huge range of μ, NB’s μ²/k term is more plausible than a single φ.

steps.title: Report
steps.body: Write the variance function in the methods. A Poisson p-value with φ̂ = 3.5 in the supplement is a contradiction, not a robustness check.

example.takeaway: Overdispersion is extra variance looking for a unit. φ̂ is a smoke alarm.

check.prompt: A Pearson φ̂ of 4 in a Poisson GLM most directly suggests:
choices: The MLE of β is inconsistent even if the mean is right
Residuals are about twice as large as Poisson V=μ expected (SEs too small if you ignore it)
check.answer: Residuals are about twice as large as Poisson V=μ expected (SEs too small if you ignore it)
check.why: √4 = 2, so residual SD is about double. Mean-model consistency can still hold.

whyWrong.The MLE of β is inconsistent even if the: Quasi/Poisson scores can still be mean-zero.

check.prompt: NB variance μ + μ²/k with μ = 10, k = 5 equals:
On the variance small-multiples, why does NB grow faster than quasi-Poisson as μ gets large?
check.figureHint: small μ vs large μ panels.
choices: Because NB variance has a μ²/k term while quasi-Poisson stays linear in μ
check.answer: Because NB variance has a μ²/k term while quasi-Poisson stays linear in μ
check.why: That is the panel’s lesson for RNA-seq-scale μ versus modest weekly counts.
